reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ESC guidelines
clinicalPearls: An inherited cardiomyopathy in which the right ventricular myocardium is progressively replaced by fibrofatty tissue, creating a substrate for ventricular arrhythmias
Frequently presents in adolescents and young adults with palpitations, syncope, or sudden cardiac death, sometimes triggered by exertion
Ventricular arrhythmias typically have a left bundle branch block morphology, reflecting their right ventricular origin
The resting ECG may show T-wave inversion in the right precordial leads and an epsilon wave, a small deflection at the end of the QRS complex
Cardiac MRI is valuable for detecting right ventricular dilatation, wall motion abnormalities, and fibrofatty infiltration
Diagnosis relies on combining imaging, ECG, arrhythmia, tissue, and family/genetic criteria rather than any single finding
Most cases follow autosomal dominant inheritance with variable penetrance, commonly linked to mutations in desmosomal proteins
Endurance exercise appears to accelerate disease progression and arrhythmic risk, so restriction from competitive and high-intensity sport is advised
reference.pathophysiology: ARVC is a genetically determined cardiomyopathy, most often caused by mutations affecting desmosomal proteins that maintain mechanical coupling between cardiomyocytes. Weakened cell-cell adhesion, aggravated by mechanical stress such as exercise, leads to myocyte death and progressive replacement of myocardium by fibrous and fatty tissue, predominantly in the right ventricle. This scarring disrupts electrical conduction, producing re-entrant ventricular arrhythmias and, over time, contractile dysfunction. Although classically right-sided, the left ventricle is commonly involved, and left-dominant and biventricular forms are increasingly recognised.
additionalDifferentials: Idiopathic right ventricular outflow tract tachycardia
Cardiac sarcoidosis with right ventricular involvement
Athlete's heart with physiological right ventricular remodelling
Congenital heart disease affecting the right ventricle (e.g. repaired tetralogy of Fallot)
additionalInvestigations: 12-lead ECG looking for right precordial T-wave inversion, epsilon waves, and prolonged terminal activation
Signal-averaged ECG to detect late potentials
Cardiac MRI for right ventricular size, function, and fibrofatty change
Echocardiography for right ventricular dilatation and regional wall motion abnormalities
Ambulatory monitoring and exercise testing to characterise ventricular arrhythmias
Genetic testing and family screening of first-degree relatives
redFlags: Exertional syncope or aborted sudden cardiac death indicating high arrhythmic risk
Sustained ventricular tachycardia with left bundle branch block morphology
Family history of premature sudden cardiac death
Progressive right or biventricular failure signalling advanced disease
reference.prognosis: The course is variable; some remain relatively stable while others suffer recurrent ventricular arrhythmias or progress to heart failure. Sudden cardiac death is the most feared outcome, and risk stratification guides use of an implantable defibrillator; overall outlook depends on arrhythmic burden and the degree of ventricular dysfunction.
pitfalls: Dismissing exertional palpitations or syncope in a young person as benign
Confusing physiological athletic remodelling with early ARVC
Relying on a normal echocardiogram to exclude the disease when MRI or ECG features are present
Failing to screen and counsel first-degree relatives and to advise exercise restriction
